# Nebius raises H100, H200, B200 and B300 GPU-hour prices from Oct 1, 2026

Nebius pricing

Teams on Nebius Hopper and Blackwell GPUs had about a week’s notice: on-demand prices for those instances go up about 17–21% from 1 October, shown in a new “Effective October 1, 2026” column on the price list. RTX PRO 6000 and L40S stay flat, and CPU-only instances rise from $0.10 to $0.13 an hour (AMD EPYC Genoa) and from $0.05 to $0.06 (Intel Ice Lake).

What it means for buyers. An 8-GPU H100 node goes from about $30.80 to $36.00 an hour on demand, so budget for the new rate from 1 October. The flat RTX PRO 6000 and L40S rates make those cards relatively cheaper for inference that does not need Hopper or Blackwell. Preemptible capacity is now billed at a floating spot price that can change as often as every 15 minutes but never exceeds one cent below the on-demand rate, so its ceiling rises with the new on-demand prices.

2026-09-23 06:08:42

results.title: Nebius Introduces Dynamic Spot Pricing for GPU VMs as AI Compute Demand Tightens | AI Industry Today
highlights:
# Nebius Introduces Dynamic Spot Pricing for GPU VMs as AI Compute Demand Tightens

Nebius is turning unused GPU capacity into a real-time compute market. From October 8, preemptible VM prices will adjust by GPU type and region as often as every 15 minutes based on available supply and customer demand, with users able either to cap the price they are willing to pay or follow the market to maximize availability. Coming just after Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates amid strong AI demand, the move shows neocloud pricing splitting into premium guaranteed capacity and dynamically priced interruptible compute — making when and where an AI workload runs an increasingly important part of compute economics.

 AI Industry Today Desk Published Sep 23, 2026 · 12:25 UTC

...

Nebius is introducing dynamic spot pricing for its preemptible virtual machines, replacing fixed discounts with market-based GPU prices that respond to real-time capacity and customer demand. Nebius said the new pricing system will take effect on October 8 and will calculate a separate spot price for each GPU type and region, giving AI developers more flexibility to trade off compute availability against cost.

Until now, Nebius priced preemptible VMs by applying discounts set by the company to its standard on-demand rates. Under the new system, an algorithm will aggregate available capacity and demand signals from Nebius customers and update the spot price as frequently as every 15 minutes. Prices will remain between a predefined floor and ceiling, with the ceiling set one cent below the corresponding on-demand GPU-hour rate.

Customers will be able to choose between two pricing strategies. Users focused on minimizing cost can set a maximum price per GPU-hour for a specific accelerator and region. If the spot price is at or below that threshold, the workload runs at the prevailing market price. If the price rises above the user’s limit, the preemptible instance stops while its data is retained and can be restarted once pricing falls back within the specified range.

Alternatively, customers can follow the market price without setting a cap, prioritizing continued access to capacity over the lowest possible cost. In that mode, users pay the dynamic spot price and generally retain their preemptible VM unless Nebius reclaims the underlying capacity or carries out maintenance. Kubernetes can automatically restart interrupted preemptible instances, while standalone VMs can be restarted manually or through Terraform, SDKs, APIs or command-line tools.

Nebius will also publish up to 30 days of spot-price history, allowing customers to identify periods of lower demand and schedule flexible workloads accordingly. The same spot price will apply across Nebius services that use preemptible capacity, including virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters and Serverless AI.

Preemptible GPU capacity is primarily intended for workloads that can tolerate interruption, including data processing, experiments, batch jobs and shorter fine-tuning runs. Nebius says only a small share of its existing preemptible workloads are actually terminated because capacity is reclaimed, with many customers completing their tasks and shutting down instances themselves. For Nebius, the model allows otherwise idle data center capacity to be monetized rather than left unused.

The change comes as AI compute remains unusually tight. Reuters reported last week that Nebius will raise on-demand prices for selected Nvidia GPUs by 17% to 21% from October 1, its second increase in three months. The company cited surging demand for infrastructure used to train and run AI models, while also raising prices on some CPU and memory resources.

Current Nebius pricing shows how large the gap between interruptible and guaranteed capacity can be. Before the dynamic system takes effect, Nebius lists preemptible B200 capacity at $3.95 per GPU-hour versus $7.15 on demand, H200 at $2.45 versus $4.50, and H100 at $2.15 versus $3.85. Those fixed preemptible rates will be replaced by the new demand-sensitive mechanism from October 8.

The shift effectively creates a more explicit market for unused AI compute inside Nebius’ cloud. When GPU supply is abundant relative to short-term demand, customers with flexible workloads may be able to access capacity at lower prices; when demand tightens, spot prices can rise toward the on-demand rate. The result moves AI infrastructure pricing closer to the model already familiar in power markets and traditional cloud computing, where interruptible capacity is priced dynamically to balance utilization and demand.

...

- Nebius on X — Spot Pricing Announcement(Official social announcement confirming that pricing will vary by GPU type, region, capacity and demand)

results.title: Spot GPU discounts run from 81.5% to nothing, September 2026
highlights:
On 2026-09-23 the discount on a spot GPU-hour runs from 81.5% at one provider down to nothing at another. Across the 42 spot rates we can set against the same provider’s own on-demand rate for the same card, the typical discount is 50%. The deepest belongs to Microsoft Azure’s H100 SXM in eastus; the shallowest are at Nebius, which since 2026-09-22 lists two of its cards at the same figure in both columns.

That last part is new. At 14:38 UTC on 2026-09-22 Nebius rewrote both columns of its price list in one go. Its H100 SXM spot rate went from $2.15 to $3.85 per GPU-hour, a rise of 79.1%; its L40S spot rate went from $0.74 to $1.55, a rise of 109.5%. Four on-demand rates moved in the same read, by 16.9% to 21.0%. The rate card at nebius.com/prices prints those figures.

## The new spot price is the old on-demand price

On every one of the six cards the arithmetic lands in the same place. Nebius listed the H100 SXM on demand at $3.85 per GPU-hour until 2026-09-22, and $3.85 is what it now asks for the same card as spot capacity. The B300 says it plainly: $7.85 was its on-demand rate before the change and is its spot rate after it, against $9.50 on demand. Where the on-demand rate did not move at all — the L40S at $1.55, the RTX PRO 6000 at $1.80 — the spot column simply came up to meet it, and the two rates are 0% apart.

results.title: Nvidia B200 Rental Prices Surge Toward $8 per GPU-Hour as Blackwell Compute Tightens | AI Industry Today
highlights:
Nvidia B200 rental compute is becoming more expensive again. The transaction-based Ornn index has risen to $7.77 per GPU-hour — up 17.1% in a month and the highest level in its public three-month window — while dedicated GPU clouds show a current median of $7.88. Different trackers report different absolute prices because they measure different provider and transaction sets, but the direction is consistent: flexible Blackwell capacity remains tight enough that B200 rental prices are rising even as newer accelerators begin entering the market.

...

Nvidia B200 rental prices have climbed toward $8 per GPU-hour as demand for Blackwell compute continues to put pressure on available cloud capacity. The transaction-based Ornn Compute Price Index for the B200 settled at $7.77 per GPU-hour on September 22, up 7.8% over seven days and 17.1% over the past month. The reading is the highest level in Ornn’s publicly available three-month history.

A separate measure of publicly listed on-demand pricing shows a similar level. GetDeploying’s latest weekly dataset puts the median B200 price across dedicated GPU clouds at $7.88 per GPU-hour, while major hyperscalers charge a median of $15.26. The $7.88 figure is therefore a provider median rather than a single transaction price or universal market average.

The distinction matters because GPU rental markets remain fragmented. Ornn calculates its benchmark from executed neocloud transactions using a volume-weighted methodology, while public-price trackers generally compare provider rate cards. Price of Compute, for example, showed a live on-demand median of $6.79 across five providers on September 23, with individual prices ranging from $5.43 at Massed Compute to $8.60 at CoreWeave.

Despite the differences in methodology, the datasets point in the same direction: premium Blackwell capacity remains expensive and recent transaction prices are rising. Ornn’s B200 benchmark has climbed from $6.64 per GPU-hour a month ago to $7.77, while its H200 index currently sits at $4.94 and H100 at $2.85. On a raw GPU-hour basis, the B200 therefore rents for about 57% more than an H200 and roughly 2.7 times the price of an H100.

...

Lambda’s public on-demand rate is around $6.69 per GPU-hour for an eight-GPU B200 configuration, while CoreWeave is listed at $8.60.

results.title: B200 vs H100 Rental Cost: Is the B200 Worth the Premium? · Aliteq
highlights: A B200 is worth its rental premium over an H100 when (1) your model or batch needs more than 80GB, so one B200 replaces two or more H100s, or (2) your workload runs on the B200 faster than the price ratio, and you keep it busy. On Nov 3, 2026 the per-GPU price ratio was 2.0× on Runpod Secure Cloud ($7.99 vs $3.99 for H100 SXM), 1.6× on Lambda ($6.99 vs $4.29, 1 GPU), 1.9× on Nebius ($8.50 vs $4.50), 1.9× on Hyperstack ($6.00 vs $3.20) and 1.4× on CoreWeave ($8.60 vs $6.16 per GPU on 8-GPU nodes). ... For small models, light use or code not yet tuned for Blackwell, the H100 is the cheaper rental.
